evidence_quotes.quote: Since 2016 in Colombia there have been “differential schemes” as a set of regulations, policies, statistical instruments and programs to promote the supply of water and sanitation in urban areas of difficult access and management, and in rural areas.
El suministro de agua en Colombia para lo urbano y lo rural responde a los denominados esquemas diferenciales.

Las organizaciones comunitarias no cumplen requisitos técnicos por los altos costos y poca oferta de asesorías profesionales, escasez de laboratorios y dificultades para el acceso a tecnologías digitales.
Las autoridades son más exigentes con los acueductos más grandes y visibles y por eso no desean formalizarse.
se sintetizaron tendencias o transformaciones de la vida rural con mayor impacto en el suministro de agua y en la gestión de los acueductos comunitarios urbano-populares y rurales
Mayor demanda de servicios de acueducto, alcantarillado y aseo que no puede ser atendida con las redes existentes.
Los ríos y quebradas están cada vez más secas y contaminadas. El agua ahora no alcanza para el suministro continuo de todos.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water supply and sanitation service access across rural, peri-urban, and urban difficult-management areas in Colombia, focusing on community aqueducts (acueductos comunitarios) and the urban-rural coverage gap.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Clearly satisfied, as the paper examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance factors shaping rural and peri-urban water supply in Colombia (normative urban-rural classifications, POT land-use plans, esquemas diferenciales, and community water governance). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Also satisfied (though embedded within a broader socio-territorial analysis of rural-urban transformations). Specifically, the paper analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms governing service access and community utility operation: (1) statutory/census territorial classifications (Ley 388 de 1997, POT) and differential service regulations (esquemas diferenciales under Decrees 1898/2016, 1272/2017, and 1688/2020) that govern permitted service levels, technologies, and provisional delivery; (2) administrative and technical compliance burdens (engineering/laboratory standards, water concessions, digital reporting requirements, mandatory micrometering, and RUPS registration) and stricter enforcement against larger/visible community aqueducts that deter formalization; and (3) weak municipal POT and environmental permitting enforcement plus flat community water quota rules strained by tourism/Airbnb and seasonal users.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains qualitative socio-legal empirical evidence from participatory fieldwork (field observations and 8 workshops/forums/encounters between November 2021 and May 2022 with leaders of community aqueducts affiliated with AMAC, Aquacol, Asatecundi, and Facoris across Quindío, Valle del Cauca, Cundinamarca, Risaralda, Cauca, and Bogotá, including normativity workshops), alongside descriptive analysis of national census/household survey (DANE, GEIH) and administrative water registries (Inventario Rural, SIASAR, RUPS). Qualitative socio-legal studies are eligible for systematic-review mechanism synthesis without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive national/rural access and formalization outcomes (97.9% urban vs. 73.3% rural aqueduct coverage; ~23% of rural population without improved water or infrastructure; only 1,078 of 21,410 collective rural systems formalized in RUPS) and qualitative community-level outcomes from fieldwork including unserved peri-urban and centro poblado demand, loss of continuous water supply, insufficient water quantity, reliance on irregular temporary supply (tanker trucks, hoses, tanks), provider non-formalization, and exclusion from water sources.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies population and units of analysis (community aqueduct organizations and rural/peri-urban communities and households in Andean Colombia—Cauca, Cundinamarca, Quindío, Risaralda, Valle del Cauca—plus national rural communities and providers in administrative registries), exposure (statutory urban-rural classifications, POT land-use rules, esquemas diferenciales regulations, and sanitary/environmental/formalization/metering rules interacting with territorial transformations), outcome (water coverage, provider formalization, service availability, continuity, and sufficiency), and study design (qualitative participatory socio-legal study with descriptive secondary registry/census analysis).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with English, Spanish, and Portuguese abstracts). Eligible under Criterion 10 because translation from the provided Spanish full text is directly feasible and the study is mechanism-relevant to differential water regulation and community utility formalization; translation method and translator must be logged in extraction_note during data extraction.

study_design: Qualitative participatory socio-legal study (field observations and 8 participatory workshops/forums with community aqueduct leaders) combined with descriptive analysis of national census, household survey, and administrative water-sector registries
population_and_sample: Community aqueduct leaders and organizations (acueductos comunitarios affiliated with AMAC, Aquacol, Asatecundi, and Facoris across 8 participatory workshops/encounters, Nov 2021–May 2022) and rural/peri-urban communities in Andean Colombia (Cauca, Cundinamarca, Quindío, Risaralda, Valle del Cauca); plus national census/GEIH households and 29,450 rural communities (912 municipalities in Rural Inventory; 10,903 communities in SIASAR; 2,127 aqueduct providers in RUPS)
exposure: Statutory/census urban-rural classifications and municipal land-use planning rules (Ley 388 de 1997, POT), differential water and sanitation regulatory schemes (esquemas diferenciales under Decrees 1898 of 2016, 1272 of 2017, and 1688 of 2020), and regulatory/administrative compliance requirements on community aqueducts (RUPS formalization, sanitary/environmental surveillance, water concessions, digital reporting, mandatory micrometering, and community water quota rules) amid urban-rural territorial transformations
outcome: Urban vs. rural aqueduct coverage, community water provider formalization (RUPS registration), ability of networks to meet demand, continuity and quantity of water supply, reliance on irregular temporary supply (tanker trucks, hoses, tanks), and community exclusion from water sources
rationale: This Spanish-language socio-legal empirical article (from the Universidad Nacional de Colombia project 'Agua y buen vivir, las organizaciones comunitarias y la normatividad en Colombia') examines rural and peri-urban water service access in Colombia through document/registry analysis and participatory fieldwork (8 workshops/forums and field observations with second-tier community aqueduct associations). Although framed broadly around urban-rural territorial transformations, it directly examines rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 readings—including statutory urban-rural classifications and POT land-use enforcement, differential service regulations (esquemas diferenciales), administrative/technical/digital compliance burdens and selective enforcement deterring community aqueduct formalization in RUPS, mandatory micrometering, water permitting, and flat community tariff quotas—and links them to water coverage, formalization, service continuity, and sufficiency outcomes. Eligible as a qualitative socio-legal study for mechanism synthesis, with Spanish translation feasible from full text per Criterion 10.
